latin.420: GAR. Verum ad istam solutionem, progrediendum est ulterius in deprecationis huius Abrahamicae consideratione. Dicimus ergo non esse simpliciter & absolute concedendum, abhorrere omnino a justitia Dei ut justi sive personaliter innocentes eadem aliquando poena involvantur cum injustis & criminosis, quantumvis inde suae deprecationis argumentum desumat Abrahamus. 1. quia Deus ipse expressis & disertis verbis testatur se contrarium aliquando facere. Ita enim Prophetam suum alloquitur, Ezech. XXI. 8. 9. Dic terrae Israelis, Sic ait Jehovah; ecce ego exeram gladium meum e vagina sua, ut exscindam ex te justum & improbum: ut exscindam ex te justum & improbum: idcirco prodibit gladius meus e vagina sua contra omnem carnem a Meridie ad Aquilonem.
latin.421: 2. Quia eius divinae dispensationis exempla quaedam Abrahamus ignorare non poterat, quae Deus omnium oculis obiecerat, primo in diluvio generali, deinde in Sodomorum subversione, tertio in Abimelechi familia, quae omnia supra suo loco produximus. PLAC. Hoc vero non est nodum solvere, sed secare. Quid si Ezech. 21 per justum intelligitur is, qui sibi, aut aliis, justus videtur, ut quibusdam placet interpretibus? Quid si justus intelligitur per comparationem cum aliis nequioribus? juxta illud Mich. 7: 4. optimus eorum est similis spinae; rectissimus prae pineto est.
latin.422: Quid, quod nullus est omnino justus, & qui non peccet: omnes peccaverunt & destituti sunt gloria Dei: ipsi infantes recens nati inhaerente vitio polluti sunt, ac propterea illis poenis digni quibus a Dei justitia afficiuntur. Taceo communes poenas aliter sese in piis habere, aliter in impiis. Illorum enim respectu sunt castigationes, & poenae paternae, & vitae peccato & miseriae obnoxiae in perfecte sanctam ac beatam commutatio; itaque nulla iis fit injuria, uti nec impiorum liberis, qui ita ob peccatum originale, quo parentibus similes sunt, moriuntur, ut tamen a multis peccatis, quae si prorogata illis vita fuisset, commisissent, & a multis calamitatibus in quas incidissent, praeserventur; id quod in aliquo beneficio reponi potest. Minime igitur pugnat hoc Dei apud Ezech. oraculum cum Abrahami testimonio. Exempla divinae dispensationis quae vir doctus subjungit, eius causae obsunt. Non enim eadem cum impiis condemnatione Noachum in diluvio generali, nec Lothum in Sodomorum subversione Dei justitia involuit. Novit enim Dominus pios e tentatione eripere, injustos autem in diem judicii poenas dantes servare: quanquam Sodomorum subversio secuta est non antecessit, ut memoria lapsus supponere videtur Vir doctus, istud Abrahami cum Deo colloquium. Idem de edito in Abimelechi familia exemplo dici debet: narratur enim eius historia demum Gen. cap. 20. & ita narratur, ut appareat idem cum Abrahamo sensisse Abimelechum de Dei justitia.
latin.423: GAR. Quomodo igitur, inquies, illud semel & iterum Capite 18. Abrahamus ingerit, abesse debere a Deo ut perimat justum cum injusto? Resp. 1. De hac Abrahae deprecatione ita indicare nonnullos, ut non modo negent, usquequaque certam esse, quam probat sententiam, sed affirment etiam multiplicem habere confutationem. Ita enim Pererius, qui ubi eam confutationem proponit, concludit tandem in hac verba. Abraham similis oratori pessimam causam defendenti, in omnes se partes versanti, ut, undecunque potest, rapiat qualecunque defensionis praesidium, miscet verba, variatque sententias, involvit rationes etiam non admodum probabiles, nec proposito suo valde congruentes, omnem demum movet lapidem, ut impetret quod a Deo postulat, non tam sententiarum pondere, aut robore argumentorum cum Deo agens, quam ardore charitatis & flagrantissimo pietatis erga miseros illos homines affectu. PLAC. Probatne, an improbat Vir doctus illa Pererii verba? Si improbat, cur laudat? Si probat, miror eum probare potuisse tam audacia, tantoque Patriarcha, patri credentium, tam injuriosa Jesuitae verba. Equidem qui me filium esse Abrahae Dei beneficio maximo credo, & laetor, vix ferre possum tam inverecunde de meo patre loquentem. Quantus enim erat Patriarcha, Dei confederatus, Dei amicus, Dei colloquio tam saepe dignatus, insignis Propheta? Quis credat eum voluisse apud Deum pessimam causam defendere, & rationibus tanquam necessariis uti minus probabilibus? Quid, quod Deus illam rationem non reprehendit, sed admisit, & nos decet credentes Patris credentium imitari fidem?
latin.424: GAR. 2. Abrahamo certa quidem fuit & immota haec regula quam nullus fidelis non agnoscit, fieri nunquam omnino posse, ut Deus injuste quidquam designet: sed in speciali videre non poterat, quomodo haec innocentium clades cum justitia Dei convenire posset. Quaerit ergo non obluctandi animo, sed ut hunc scrupulum sibi eximat, an Deus justum perditurus sit cum impio. Sic. PLAC. Suntne igitur illa verba dubitantis, aut simpliciter quaerentis, Abfit tibi ut facias tale quidpiam, morti tradendo justum cum injusto, ut ita sit justo sicut injusto: Abfit tibi. An judex totius terrae non exerceret jus? Quae sunt assertiones vehementes ac fortes, tanquam certae & indubitatae, si hae non sunt? Certe igitur sciebat, nec Deum posse quicquam inique designare, nec justum esse apud Deum judicem, ut pariter justus ac injustus damnetur, itaque hoc unum flagitabat, non modo ut Deus justos propter impios non damnaret, id quod ei videbatur nimis a Dei justitia alienum, sed ut propter paucos justos parceret vel impiis, vel saltem ipsi loco seu urbi, id quod Dei bonitatem summam non dedecere videbatur. Agebatur enim non de qualicunque castigatione, sed de poena judiciaria, & quodammodo aeterna: cuiusmodi poena certum est nunquam justos propter impios puniri.
latin.425: GAR. 3. Cum Deus in exequendis judiciis suis, aliquando ex justitiae rigore agat, aliquando justitiam aequitate temperet, dico Abrahamum, pro charitate sua in Sodomitas, percupiisse, ut Deus judicium illud aliqua misericordiae testificatione temperaret: Itaque seposito nunc quidem Dei rigorosiori modo, unice haesisse in ordinaria & communiori justitiae divinae dispensatione, cum praesertim alte animo ipsius insideret foedus illud cum ipso nuper initum Gen. 17. nimirum foedus gratiae, in quo Deus promisit se non imputaturum aliena peccata, Ierem. XXXI. 29. 30. Et cujus foederis nonnullam aliquando suavitatem etiam iis exhibet, qui ad illud non pertinent. PLAC. Duae sunt partes orationis Abrahami: altera asserit non convenire justitiae Dei, ut justus pereat cum impio: altera petit a Deo, ut propter paucos justos parcat urbi; id quod, fateor, non exspectaretur esse, sed testificationem potius misericordiae: itaque haec pars ad rem quam agimus non facit. Ab altera illa ductum est argumentum nostrum, quae est non aequitati modo, sed rigori etiam justitiae, omni ex parte congruens. Quare quo spectet ista responsio, & quid argumento meo afferat novi, nullus video. Illud tantum reponam, Si in foedere gratiae Deus promisit se non imputaturum aliena peccata, igitur cum nobis non imputare peccatum actuale primum Adami: Quomodo ergo nos ob illud peccatum punit, inflictâ scilicet poena judiciaria, nempe corruptione originali? Caeterum non eo inficias, quin Deus nonnunquam eadem condemnatione temporali pios cum impiis involvat; quippe, nullus est ita pius & justus, ut non peccet interdum, & pii non, uti par est, eorum, quibus admixti sunt, peccata detestantur fugiunt, redarguunt. Interim tamen huiusmodi calamitates cedunt piis in castigationes paternas, quibus cavetur ne aeternum pereant cum impiis. Nos autem in hac causa de imputatione judiciaria agimus & damnatione ad poenas proprie dictas & justitiae satisfactorias, quales illae sunt quas lex comminatur & justitia, ut sibi satisfiat, exigit, quas ob aliena peccata portare innocentes minime nocentium vades, contendimus cum Abrahae testimonio, cum Dei justitia & aequitate pugnare.

pass_a.420: GAR pushes past Placeus's solution: one must not simply and absolutely concede that it wholly abhors God's justice for the just—or personally innocent—ever to be wrapped in the same penalty with the unjust and criminal, even though Abraham draws his plea from that. First proof: God himself in express words testifies he sometimes does the contrary. He addresses his prophet, Ezek. 21:8–9: Say to the land of Israel, Thus says Jehovah; behold, I will draw my sword from its sheath to cut off from you the just and the wicked—therefore my sword will go out against all flesh from south to north.
pass_a.421: Second: Abraham could not have been ignorant of divine-dispensation examples God had set before all eyes—the general flood, the overthrow of Sodom, Abimelech's household—already produced above. Placeus: that does not untie the knot but cuts it. What if in Ezek. 21 'the just' means one who seems just to himself or others, as some interpreters like? Or just only by comparison with worse men, per Mic. 7:4—the best of them like a thorn, the most upright worse than a thorn-hedge?
pass_a.422: Besides, no one is wholly just or without sin: all have sinned and lack God's glory; even newborns are polluted by inherent vice and so worthy of the penalties God's justice lays on them. Shared calamities also differ: for the pious they are paternal chastisements and a commute of a sin-bound life into perfect holiness—no injury—and wicked men's children dying for original sin are spared many later sins and woes. So Ezekiel's oracle does not clash with Abraham. GAR's examples hurt his own cause: Noah was not condemned with the wicked in the flood, nor Lot in Sodom's fall—the Lord knows to rescue the godly and keep the unjust for judgment day. Sodom's overthrow followed, did not precede, Abraham's colloquy; Abimelech's story is Gen. 20 and shows Abimelech shared Abraham's sense of God's justice.
pass_a.423: GAR asks how Abraham twice in Gen. 18 insists God must not destroy just with unjust. Reply 1: some treat Abraham's plea as not wholly sure and multiply confutations. Pererius concludes Abraham is like an orator defending a bad cause—twisting every way, mixing words, using weak reasons, moving every stone—acting with God less by argument weight than by charity's heat toward those wretched men. Placeus: does the learned man approve or disapprove Pererius? If he disapproves, why praise? If he approves, Placeus marvels he could approve such bold Jesuit insults to the patriarch, father of believers. Placeus, glad to be Abraham's son by God's gift, can barely bear such shameless talk of his father. How great was that confederate and friend of God, so often honored with God's talk, a marked prophet? Who believes he meant to defend a worst cause before God with less-probable reasons as if necessary? God did not rebuke that reason but admitted it, and believers ought to imitate the father of believers' faith.
pass_a.424: GAR 2: Abraham held the sure rule every believer owns—God can never appoint anything unjust—but in the special case he could not see how the innocents' ruin fit God's justice, so he asks not to fight God but to clear his scruple whether God will destroy the just with the wicked. Placeus: are 'Far be it from you to do such a thing… Far be it from you. Shall the Judge of all the earth not do right?' the words of a doubter or mere inquirer? If these are not vehement sure assertions, what are? Abraham knew God cannot appoint iniquity and that before God as judge it is not just that just and unjust be damned alike; he begged not only that God not damn the just for the unjust—too alien to God's justice—but that for a few just he spare the wicked or at least the place. The matter was not any chastisement but judicial, somehow eternal, punishment—and of that kind the just are never punished for the unjust.
pass_a.425: GAR 3: when God executes judgments he sometimes acts from justice's rigor, sometimes tempers justice with equity; Abraham, for love of the Sodomites, longed that God temper that judgment with some witness of mercy—so, setting aside the more rigorous mode, he clung to the ordinary commoner dispensation of divine justice, especially with the recent Gen. 17 grace-covenant deep in mind, in which God promised not to impute others' sins (Jer. 31:29–30), and whose sweetness he sometimes shows even to outsiders. Placeus: Abraham's speech has two parts—one asserts it does not fit God's justice that the just perish with the wicked; the other asks God to spare the city for a few just—that second is mercy's witness, not our case. Our argument is drawn from the first, which fits not only equity but justice's rigor throughout. So Placeus sees nothing new this reply adds. He only returns: if in the grace-covenant God promised not to impute others' sins, then he does not impute Adam's first actual sin to us—how then punish us for it with judicial original corruption? He does not deny God sometimes wraps the pious in the same temporal condemnation with the wicked—none is so pious as never to sin, and the pious often fail to flee mixed men's sins—yet such calamities become paternal chastisements keeping them from perishing eternally with the wicked. But this cause concerns judicial imputation and damnation to proper satisfactory penalties the law threatens—which innocents as sureties of the guiltless must not bear for others' sins: with Abraham's testimony that clashes with God's justice and equity. Tip before the fourth king-analogy.

420: GAR. But against that solution one must go further in considering this Abrahamic deprecation. We say, then, that it is not to be conceded simply and absolutely that it wholly abhors God's justice that the just, or personally innocent, should sometimes be involved in the same penalty with the unjust and criminal, however much Abraham takes from that the argument of his plea. 1. because God himself testifies in express and clear words that he sometimes does the contrary. For so he addresses his prophet, Ezek. 21:8–9: Say to the land of Israel, Thus says Jehovah; behold, I will draw my sword from its sheath, that I may cut off from you the just and the wicked: that I may cut off from you the just and the wicked: therefore my sword shall go forth from its sheath against all flesh from the South to the North.
421: 2. Because Abraham could not have been ignorant of certain examples of that divine dispensation which God had set before the eyes of all—first in the general flood, then in the overthrow of Sodom, third in Abimelech's household—all of which we produced above in their place. PLAC. But this is not to untie the knot, but to cut it. What if in Ezek. 21 by 'the just' is meant one who seems just to himself or to others, as it pleases some interpreters? What if 'just' is understood by comparison with others more wicked?—according to that word of Mic. 7:4: the best of them is like a thorn; the most upright is worse than a thorn-hedge.
422: What of this—that there is no one at all who is just and who does not sin: all have sinned and are destitute of the glory of God: even infants newly born are polluted by inherent vice, and therefore worthy of those penalties with which they are afflicted by God's justice. I pass over that common penalties stand otherwise in the pious, otherwise in the impious. For in respect of the former they are chastisements and paternal penalties, and a commuting of a life liable to sin and misery into one perfectly holy and blessed; so no injury is done them—nor to the children of the impious, who so die for original sin, by which they are like their parents, that they are yet preserved from many sins they would have committed if life had been prolonged to them, and from many calamities into which they would have fallen; which can be counted for some benefit. Least of all, then, does this oracle of God in Ezekiel clash with Abraham's testimony. The examples of divine dispensation which the learned man subjoins stand against his cause. For God's justice did not involve Noah in the same condemnation with the impious in the general flood, nor Lot in the overthrow of Sodom. For the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished: although the overthrow of Sodom followed and did not precede—as the learned man's slip of memory seems to suppose—that colloquy of Abraham with God. The same must be said of the example published in Abimelech's household: for its history is narrated only at Gen. 20, and is so narrated that Abimelech appears to have felt the same as Abraham concerning God's justice.
423: GAR. How then, you will say, does Abraham once and again in chapter 18 press that it ought to be far from God to destroy the just with the unjust? Reply 1. Some so treat this deprecation of Abraham that they not only deny the opinion he proves is altogether certain, but even affirm it has a manifold confutation. So Pererius, who when he sets out that confutation concludes at last in these words: Abraham, like an orator defending a worst cause, turning himself every way so that from wherever he can he may snatch any shield of defense, mixes words and varies sentences, wraps in reasons not very probable nor much fitting his purpose, and finally moves every stone to obtain what he asks of God, dealing with God not so much by the weight of sentences or the strength of arguments as by the heat of charity and the most burning affection of piety toward those wretched men. PLAC. Does the learned man approve, or disapprove, those words of Pererius? If he disapproves, why does he praise them? If he approves, I marvel that he could approve words so bold, and so injurious to so great a Patriarch, the father of believers, from a Jesuit. For my part, who by God's greatest gift believe myself a son of Abraham and rejoice in it, I can scarcely bear one speaking so shamelessly of my father. For how great was the Patriarch, confederate of God, friend of God, so often honored with God's colloquy, a distinguished Prophet? Who would believe he meant to defend a worst cause before God, and to use less probable reasons as if they were necessary? What of this—that God did not rebuke that reason but admitted it, and it becomes us believers to imitate the faith of the Father of believers?
424: GAR. 2. To Abraham this rule was indeed certain and unmoved, which no believer fails to acknowledge—that it can never at all come to pass that God should appoint anything unjust: but in the special case he could not see how this slaughter of innocents could agree with God's justice. He asks, therefore, not with a mind to resist, but that he may clear this scruple for himself, whether God is about to destroy the just with the wicked. So. PLAC. Are those then the words of one doubting, or simply asking: Far be it from you to do any such thing, delivering the just to death with the unjust, so that it should be with the just as with the unjust: Far be it from you. Shall the Judge of all the earth not do right? What are vehement and strong assertions, as certain and undoubted, if these are not? He knew for certain, then, both that God cannot appoint anything iniquitous, and that it is not just before God as judge that the just and the unjust be damned alike; and so he begged this one thing—not only that God should not damn the just for the sake of the unjust, which seemed to him too alien from God's justice, but that for the sake of a few just he should spare even the unjust, or at least the place or city itself, which seemed not unworthy of God's highest goodness. For the matter was not about any chastisement whatever, but about judicial punishment, and in a manner eternal: of which kind of punishment it is certain the just are never punished for the sake of the unjust.
425: GAR. 3. Since God, in executing his judgments, sometimes acts from the rigor of justice, sometimes tempers justice with equity, I say Abraham, for his charity toward the Sodomites, earnestly desired that God would temper that judgment with some testimony of mercy: and so, setting aside for now God's more rigorous mode, he clung only to the ordinary and more common dispensation of divine justice—especially since that covenant lately struck with him in Gen. 17 sat deep in his mind, namely the covenant of grace, in which God promised he would not impute others' sins, Jer. 31:29–30. And of which covenant he sometimes shows some sweetness even to those who do not belong to it. PLAC. There are two parts of Abraham's speech: one asserts that it does not agree with God's justice that the just perish with the wicked; the other asks of God that for the sake of a few just he spare the city—which, I confess, would not be looked for as due, but rather as a testimony of mercy: so this part does not serve the matter we are treating. From that other part our argument is drawn, which agrees not only with equity but also with the rigor of justice in every respect. So what this reply aims at, and what new thing it brings to my argument, I see none. I will only reply this: If in the covenant of grace God promised he would not impute others' sins, then he does not impute to us Adam's first actual sin: How then does he punish us for that sin, namely by inflicting a judicial penalty—original corruption? For the rest I do not deny that God sometimes involves the pious in the same temporal condemnation with the impious; for no one is so pious and just that he does not sometimes sin, and the pious do not, as they ought, detest, flee, and rebuke the sins of those among whom they are mixed. Meanwhile, however, calamities of this kind become for the pious paternal chastisements by which it is provided that they not perish eternally with the impious. But we in this cause are treating of judicial imputation and damnation to penalties properly so called and satisfactory to justice—such as those the law threatens and justice, that it may be satisfied, exacts—which innocents, least of all as sureties of the guiltless, we contend with Abraham's testimony clash with God's justice and equity when borne for others' sins.
